section.title: Against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia
section.sectionRationale: With Jerusalem now fallen, Ezekiel turns from Judah's own sin to the nations who gloated over her ruin. Four short oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia share one refrain, that they will know the LORD is God, showing that His sovereignty and justice reach every nation, not Israel alone.
section.thesis: The LORD who judged His own covenant people for their sin also judges the nations for their contempt and vengeance against her, proving that His justice plays no favorites and that every nation, Israel included, is accountable to Him alone.
section.frameNote: Four short oracles in turn: against Ammon for gloating over the temple's fall; against Moab for treating Judah as just another nation; against Edom for vengeful violence; and against Philistia for age old, malicious hostility.

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, set your face against the Ammonites and prophesy against them.

Tell the Ammonites to hear the word of the Lord GOD, for this is what the Lord GOD says: 'Because you exclaimed, “Aha!” when My {{miqdash|sanctuary}} was profaned, when the land of Israel was laid waste, and when the house of Judah went into exile,
therefore I will indeed give you as a possession to the people of the East. They will set up their camps and pitch their tents among you. They will eat your fruit and drink your milk.
I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels, and Ammon a resting place for sheep. Then you will know that {{yada|I am the LORD}}.'
For this is what the Lord GOD says: 'Because you clapped your hands and stomped your feet and rejoiced over the land of Israel with a heart full of contempt,

therefore I will indeed stretch out My hand against you and give you as plunder to the nations. I will cut you off from the peoples and exterminate you from the countries. I will destroy you, and you will know that I am the LORD.'

units.label: Against Moab
units.note: Judah reduced to a common nation

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: 'Because Moab and Seir said, “Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,”
therefore I will indeed expose the flank of Moab beginning with its frontier cities, Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim, the glory of the land.
I will give it along with the Ammonites as a possession to the people of the East, so that the Ammonites will no longer be remembered among the nations.
So I will execute judgments on Moab, and they will know that I am the LORD.'
This is what the Lord GOD says: 'Because Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah, and in so doing incurred grievous guilt,

therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will stretch out My hand against Edom and cut off from it both man and beast. I will make it a wasteland, and from Teman to Dedan they will fall by the sword.
I will take My {{naqam|vengeance}} on Edom by the hand of My people Israel, and they will deal with Edom according to My anger and wrath. Then they will know My vengeance, declares the Lord GOD.'
This is what the Lord GOD says: 'Because the Philistines acted in vengeance, taking vengeance with malice of soul to destroy Judah with ancient hostility,
therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, I will stretch out My hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the remnant along the coast.
I will execute great vengeance against them with furious reproof. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay My vengeance upon them.'”

miqdash.gloss: Sanctuary or holy place, the temple itself. Ammon's mockery was not merely political gloating over a rival's defeat but derision aimed at the dwelling place of the LORD, which He takes as a direct affront to Himself.

yada.gloss: To know, in the sense of firsthand, undeniable recognition. The refrain 'then you will know that I am the LORD' recurs after every oracle in this chapter, the goal of judgment being not mere destruction but the unmistakable revelation of who God is, even to nations who never called on His name.

naqam.gloss: Vengeance or retribution. Edom and Philistia are judged for taking naqam of their own into their own hands with malice; the LORD answers by taking His own naqam, reserving to Himself the right to repay evil that belongs to Him alone, Deuteronomy 32:35.

basic.context: With Jerusalem's fall now certain, Ezekiel's attention turns outward to four neighboring nations, Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia, each of whom responded to Judah's disaster with contempt, opportunism, or old grudges rather than sorrow. Each oracle follows the same short pattern: an accusation, a sentence, and the refrain that they will know the LORD is God.
basic.hermeneutics: These are real historical judgments pronounced on real neighboring peoples for real, specific sins named in the text, mostly fulfilled through later Babylonian and Arab incursions into these territories. The passage is not a template for how to treat modern national rivals but a description of God's actual justice on these ancient nations for gloating, greed, vengeance, and old hostility.
basic.originalLanguages: Ammon mocked the miqdash, the very sanctuary of God, treating His holy dwelling as fair game for scorn. Edom and Philistia are condemned for taking naqam, vengeance, into their own hands; the LORD answers by taking His own vengeance, since retribution belongs to Him. And every oracle ends the same way: they will yada, know, undeniably, that the LORD is God.
basic.typology: The repeated refrain, that the nations will know the LORD, anticipates the wider biblical hope that God's justice and glory will be made known to all peoples, not Israel only, a hope that finds its fullest answer in the gospel going out to every nation in Christ's name.
basic.christ: These oracles show a God whose justice extends to every nation, refusing to let gloating over His people's suffering go unanswered; this same God, in Christ, would later bear the world's contempt and violence Himself on the cross, absorbing what these nations were condemned for dishing out, and offering forgiveness even to hostile peoples like Philistia and Edom's descendants.
basic.god: God is impartial: He judges His own covenant people for sin, and just as surely judges the nations for gloating over that judgment, for treachery, for vengeance, and for ancient malice. His justice is never selective, and His purpose in every act of judgment is that all these peoples come to know Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 15 to 16 and Jeremiah 48 give companion oracles against Moab; Jeremiah 49 addresses Ammon, Edom, and Philistia similarly. Obadiah is devoted entirely to Edom's judgment for gloating over Judah's fall. Romans 12:19 echoes 'vengeance is Mine, I will repay', quoting Deuteronomy 32:35, the same principle at work in these oracles against Edom and Philistia.
basic.oneStory: God's justice does not stop at Israel's border; it reaches every nation that mocked, plundered, or took vengeance against His suffering people. This anticipates the day when every knee, from every nation once judged, will bow and know that the LORD is God, a knowledge the gospel now carries to the very peoples once condemned here.

context.literary:
Ezekiel 25 is a hinge. Chapters 1 to 24 are about Jerusalem, and the last of them ends with the prophet struck dumb, told that his mouth will be opened only when a fugitive arrives with news of the city's fall, Ezekiel 24:27. That arrival is reported in Ezekiel 33:21-22. Everything between, chapters 25 to 32, is spoken into that silence, and it is arranged by theme rather than by date. Seven nations are addressed: Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia here, then Tyre and Sidon, then Egypt at length. The number is probably deliberate, a full and complete reckoning with Judah's neighbours.

The four oracles in this chapter are built on one hinge word. Each accusation opens with 'because' and each sentence with 'therefore', verses 3 to 4, 6 to 7, 8 to 9, 12 to 13 and 15 to 16. Ammon gets two such pairs, which matches the two things it did, one with its voice and one with its hands and feet. The pattern is a prophetic lawsuit in miniature: here is the offence, here is the matching penalty. The punishment is meant to be read as fitting the crime. Ammon crowed over a sanctuary laid waste and is itself handed over to desert raiders. Edom took vengeance and has the LORD's vengeance returned.

The oracles also move in a deliberate order. The first two nations east of the Jordan, Ammon and Moab, are close kin of Israel through Lot, Genesis 19:36-38. Edom, southeast, is kin through Esau. Philistia, on the western coast, is the only one with no family tie, and its oracle is placed last and marked as the climax. The accusation sharpens as it travels from mocking words, to a sneer, to vengeful violence, to a long malice.

Finally, notice what Ezekiel leaves out. Ammon, Moab and Edom are not charged with idolatry or with the violence of empire. Their sin is a posture toward the people of God in the hour of disaster.
context.historical:
The rise and fall of these small states is the background. Ammon, Moab and Edom were Judah's near neighbours, and in the final years before 586 BC they were drawn into the politics of revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah 27:3 records envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon arriving in Jerusalem to plan resistance together. The coalition came to nothing, and when Babylon moved, these states either stood aside or joined the winning side.

The charge against Ammon is concrete. After Jerusalem fell, Baalis king of the Ammonites sent Ishmael to murder Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had appointed, Jeremiah 40:14, and Ishmael carried captives from Mizpah toward Ammon, Jeremiah 41:10. Ezekiel had already seen Babylon's sword choosing between two roads, one to Jerusalem and the other to Rabbah, Ezekiel 21:20. So Ammon's gloating was dangerous complacency; it thought itself spared.

The 'people of the East' of verse 4 are the tent-dwelling peoples of the eastern desert, the same ones who raided Israel's harvests in the days of the judges, Judges 6:3. Moab's frontier towns in verse 9, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim and Beth-jeshimoth, sit on the plateau where Israel's tribes had once settled, Numbers 32:37-38 and 33:49. Opening those towns to attack exposes the whole country behind them.

Edom's guilt is documented elsewhere. Obadiah 11 to 12 accuses Edom of standing aloof when foreigners entered Jerusalem's gate and of gloating over Judah's destruction, and Psalm 137:7 remembers Edom urging the destroyers on. Teman and Dedan in verse 13 mark Edom's heartland and its southern trading frontier.

Philistia's quarrel with Israel was among the oldest. The Cherethites of verse 16 were a Philistine-linked people on the coast, 1 Samuel 30:14, and Amos 9:7 says the Philistines came from Caphtor. In later centuries the Edomite lands were taken over by Arab peoples, and Malachi 1:2 to 5 already speaks of Edom's hill country laid waste.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a long line of oracles against the nations. Amos opened his book with a cycle against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom and Ammon, Amos 1:3 to 2:3. Isaiah 13 to 23 collects burdens on the nations, and Jeremiah 46 to 51 gathers another group, with Jeremiah 48 and 49 addressing Moab, Ammon and Edom in close parallel. Ezekiel is working inside an established genre, and he is aware of it.

The great text on Edom is Obadiah, which says what Ezekiel 25:12 to 14 says at length, and Ezekiel 35 returns to Edom's hill country, Mount Seir, with a full oracle that names Edom's 'ancient hatred', Ezekiel 35:5. The two prophets read each other.

The deepest root is Deuteronomy 32:35, 'Vengeance is Mine', and Leviticus 19:18, which forbids God's people to seek revenge. Paul brings both together in Romans 12:19, telling believers to leave room for God's wrath. That is exactly the line these oracles draw: when Edom takes vengeance, it steals what belongs to God, and God takes it back.

The oracles are not the last word on these nations. Isaiah 11:14 sees them subdued under the Messiah's rule. Amos 9:12 says the restored house of David will possess 'the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name', and James quotes that very promise at the Jerusalem council, Acts 15:16-17, to show that the Gentiles are being included. Psalm 87:4 lists Philistia among the nations of whom the LORD says, 'This one was born in Zion.' Zechariah 9:7 even promises that a Philistine remnant will be like a clan in Judah. The judgment is real, and it is not the only story.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel is speaking to exiles who had just watched the temple burn and heard their neighbours cheer. A people in that position are tempted to two errors. One is to conclude that the gods of the neighbours are stronger. The other is to conclude that God has simply stopped caring. These four short oracles are meant to cut off both.

First, the prophet wanted the exiles to hear that the LORD had marked every cheer. Ammon's 'Aha' was heard, Moab's remark that Judah was no different from anyone else was heard, Edom's bloodthirst and Philistia's old malice were all heard. Nothing said over Jerusalem's ruins was lost on Him.

Second, he wanted them to understand that Judah's discipline did not make her enemies righteous. The same God who had judged His people with a firm hand now turns to those who trampled them while they lay down. Judgment on Judah and judgment on the nations are not rivals. Both come from one holy God.

Third, he wanted them to leave vengeance where it belongs. The exiles are not told to take up arms against Edom. They are told that the LORD will see to it. That frees a wounded people from bitterness and keeps their hope fixed on Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These oracles describe what the LORD announced against particular nations at a particular time, for specific named offences. They are not a licence for any nation or any believer to treat a neighbour as a target, and they are not a forecast about modern countries that happen to occupy the same land. To read them that way would repeat the very mistake of Edom and Philistia, taking vengeance into human hands.

Notice, too, that when verse 14 says Israel will carry out the sentence on Edom, the text calls it 'My vengeance' and 'according to My anger and wrath'. Israel acts as the LORD's instrument, not on her own initiative or for her own grudge. The command that does carry forward is the one Scripture states elsewhere: believers do not avenge themselves, but leave room for God's wrath, Romans 12:19, and they love their enemies, Matthew 5:44.

What also carries forward is a plain principle about gloating. To rejoice when someone suffers, even someone who has wronged us, is to stand where Ammon stood. Proverbs 24:17 says, 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls.' The chapter teaches that the Judge hears the laughter.

debates.question: Why does God judge these four nations for essentially the same kind of sin, but does not always specify what made their guilt 'grievous' compared to Israel's own sin, judged at much greater length in earlier chapters?

views.label: The brevity reflects a real difference in covenant relationship
views.case: Israel had received the law, the temple, and prophetic warning for centuries, so her sin carried a depth these nations, who never had such privilege, did not share; the shorter oracles reflect real proportion in accountability, not indifference.

views.label: The brevity reflects genre and audience, not lesser seriousness
views.case: These are stylized, formulaic nation oracles meant to be memorable and repeated aloud to exiles who needed reassurance quickly, not full covenant lawsuits; the compressed form does not mean the sin was lightly regarded, since the LORD still calls Edom's guilt 'grievous', verse 12.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms that God's justice is proportioned to what each people knew and did, and that no nation, however briefly addressed, escapes real accountability before Him.

debates.question: How should the 'people of the East' receiving Ammon and Moab, and Israel carrying out vengeance on Edom, be understood as fulfilled?

views.label: Fulfilled in the Babylonian and then Arab pressure that followed the exile
views.case: Ammon and Moab were weakened by Babylon and then overrun by desert peoples from the east, which matches the camps, tents and camels of verses 4 and 5. The sources about Edom show it being displaced in later centuries by Arab peoples, and Malachi 1:2 to 5 already speaks of Edom's land laid waste.

views.label: Israel's role against Edom points past the exile to a later and larger fulfilment
views.case: Verse 14 says the vengeance on Edom comes by the hand of 'My people Israel'. That does not fit the Babylonian period, when Judah was in ruins. Readers who hold this point to later Jewish campaigns against the Edomites, to Numbers 24:18 and Amos 9:12, and to the prophets' hope that Edom's remnant would one day be possessed in a fuller, messianic way.

debates.bearing: The text itself is brief on how and when, and this humility is wise. In either reading the point stands: the sentence is carried out by the LORD, through human agents He chooses, and the aim is that they know Him.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the little word that opens verse 3, 'Aha', in Hebrew he'ach. It is an exclamation of delighted contempt. The Psalms use it of enemies who watch the righteous fall, Psalm 35:21, and Ezekiel hears the same cry from Tyre, Ezekiel 26:2, and from the enemy over Israel's heights, Ezekiel 36:2. It is a sound before it is an argument, and the prophet makes the LORD quote it back to the nation that made it. In verse 6 the contempt becomes bodily: clapping hands and stamping feet, the very gestures the LORD had commanded Ezekiel to make over Israel's own abominations, Ezekiel 6:11. Ammon turns a sign of judgment into a dance.

The sentences against Ammon, Edom and Philistia all share the verb 'cut off', karat, in verses 7, 13 and 16. It is the ordinary Hebrew verb for 'cut' and also the verb used for making a covenant, 'cutting' a covenant. Here it is the other cut, the covenant sanction, as the LORD severs a people from the land of the living. The phrase 'stretch out My hand' in verses 7, 13 and 16 is the language of the exodus plagues, Exodus 7:5. The God who once stretched out His hand on Egypt for Israel's sake now does so for Israel's sake again.

The word naqam, 'vengeance', is the hinge of verses 12 to 17. It is what Edom and Philistia took and what the LORD takes back. It is the same word that Leviticus 19:18 forbids to the people of God, 'Do not seek revenge', and that Deuteronomy 32:35 reserves to the LORD. The translation 'vengeance' can sound petty to modern ears; the Hebrew idea is of a just and public redress that only a rightful judge may carry out.

In verse 15 the 'ancient hostility' is the phrase Ezekiel 35:5 uses of Edom, 'ancient hatred'. The English reader is given a rare cross link: Edom and Philistia are accused of the same long grudge, and the prophet reuses the phrase. The phrase 'malice of soul' joins nefesh, the soul as appetite and inner life, to an ill intention, so the hostility is not only an act but a settled desire.

Finally, the closing word of each oracle, 'they will know that I am the LORD', is the recognition formula Ezekiel uses again and again. Here it is said of nations. The verb is yada, to know by experience, as one knows a person. To know the LORD is to meet Him, either in judgment or in grace.

typology.type: Ammon's gloating over the sanctuary, Ezekiel 25:3
typology.fulfillment: Ammon cried 'Aha' as the sanctuary was profaned. At the cross the onlookers shake their heads and mock, 'He saved others; let Him save Himself', Matthew 27:39-44, echoing Psalm 22:7. The temple Ammon mocked was a building; the one mocked at Calvary is the true temple, whose body Jesus said would be raised in three days, John 2:19-21. The escalation is that the Son who is mocked answers not with the sword of verse 7 but with prayer for His mockers, Luke 23:34. The type falls short because Ammon's mockery was met with judgment, while the mockery at Calvary was met with forgiveness bought by the very death that was mocked.

Edom, the nation of Esau, is the standing example of brother turned against brother, Obadiah 10. The pattern recurs in Herod the Great, an Idumean, which is the Greek name for Edomite, who tried to kill the child born King of the Jews, Matthew 2:16. The line of Esau rises again against the line of promise. In Christ the escalation is that the promised Seed is not destroyed but survives to take the kingdom, and Obadiah 21 sees 'deliverers' going up Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau, so that 'the kingdom will belong to the LORD'. The type is limited: Edom's story is not only hostility, since Amos 9:12 promises that a remnant of Edom will be possessed within the house of David's restoration.

typology.type: Philistia and the nations brought into Zion
typology.fulfillment: Philistia was the oldest foe, and the oracle ends on her destruction. Yet the prophets reverse the picture. Zechariah 9:7 promises that a Philistine remnant 'will become a remnant for our God', like a clan in Judah, and Psalm 87:4 pictures Philistia, Tyre and Cush among those of whom the LORD says, 'This one was born in Zion.' The fulfilment comes in the gospel to the nations, as Philip meets a man from the Ethiopian court on the Gaza road, Acts 8:26-39. The correspondence is that judgment clears the way for inclusion. It falls short only in that a people is never saved as a people by their history; each is saved by being gathered into Christ.

typology.type: The refrain 'they will know that I am the LORD'
typology.fulfillment: The repeated recognition formula looks ahead to a time when knowing the LORD is no longer the fruit of judgment but of grace. Jeremiah 31:34 promises that all will know Him, from the least to the greatest, and Isaiah 11:9 says the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. In Christ that promise begins, since to know the Father is to know the Son, John 17:3. The type is incomplete until the day every tongue confesses, Philippians 2:10-11.

study.christ:
These oracles lead to Christ chiefly by contrast and by promise. They are first of all about vengeance, and Christ is the one who stands where vengeance is the issue.

The first link is a deliberate omission. When Jesus read from Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth, He stopped partway through a sentence. Isaiah 61:2 reads 'to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor and the day of our God's vengeance', and Luke 4:18-19 reports only the first half. The day of vengeance is real, and the oracles of Ezekiel 25 show it, but the first coming of Christ is the year of favour. Christ does not abolish the justice of these oracles; He postpones its final stroke in order to offer mercy first.

The second link is the cross. These nations are condemned for contempt, for gloating and for violence toward God's people. At Calvary every one of those sins is turned on the Son of God Himself. He is mocked, struck and left to die, and from the cross He prays, 'Father, forgive them', Luke 23:34. What Ammon, Edom and Philistia did to a people, humanity did to the Holy One, and the answer is not the sword of Ezekiel 25:7 but a prayer. Paul says of His people that while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, Romans 5:10, and that is the story of these nations too.

The third link is the promise that these very nations will be gathered. Amos 9:12 speaks of possessing the remnant of Edom, and Acts 15:16-17 reads it as being fulfilled as the Gentiles turn to the Lord. Zechariah 9:7 gives the same hope for Philistia, and Psalm 87:4 for Philistia and Tyre. Christ is the one in whom the son of David's house is restored, and in Him people from Edom and Ammon and Philistia come to know the LORD in mercy, not only in judgment.

A caution keeps this honest. Ezekiel 25 does not mention the Messiah, and its details are not coded pictures of Jesus. The links are made by the way the New Testament uses the same themes: vengeance belongs to God, the one who bears the contempt of enemies is the Son, and the nations are included. Hebrews 10:30 even quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 as a warning, so the passage also tells us that to reject the one who bore the cross is to meet the vengeance He postponed.
study.god:
The first thing these oracles show is that the God of Israel is not tribal. He is the LORD of Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia too, and the sentences are His. No nation stands outside His hearing. This is the same God who had just judged His own people at length, and He does not exempt them because they are His. Yet the oracles also show that He does not exempt their enemies because He used them. The Babylonian sword that struck Jerusalem was His instrument, and the nations who gloated were not His instruments but His opponents, and they are held to account for their own delight.

God is attentive. Ammon's 'Aha' was a sound spoken in private celebration, probably forgotten within a season, and it is preserved here word for word. He hears the claps and the stamping, the careless remark that Judah is like all the nations, the long quiet grudge. This is both frightening and comforting. For the exiles, it means that every insult they endured was seen. For the nations, it means that contempt is not weightless.

God is just, and His justice is proportioned. Each sentence matches the offence. Ammon crowed over a sanctuary laid waste and will be laid waste, a pasture for camels. Edom and Philistia took vengeance and receive it. Edom's sentence names Israel as the agent, fitting the family quarrel at the root of the offence. Justice here is not random violence but fitting, public and measured.

God is jealous for what is His. Ammon despised His sanctuary, and Moab denied that Judah had any distinct place among the nations. Yet Numbers 23:9 describes Israel as a people dwelling apart and not reckoned among the nations. Moab's claim that Judah is like everyone else strikes at the calling God put on His people. To dismiss the holiness of God's people is to dismiss the God whose people they are.

Finally, He aims at being known. Every oracle ends, 'they will know that I am the LORD.' Even judgment is revelation. For worship, the passage teaches us to take vengeance out of our hands and put it in His. We can pray with a clean conscience about those who have wronged us, because the Judge hears, sees and answers, and He is also the God of the cross.

crossReferences.note: The fullest companion to the Edom oracle. Obadiah charges Edom with standing aloof while strangers entered Jerusalem's gate, gloating over Judah's disaster, and Ezekiel 25:12 sums up the same offence as acting vengefully. The two prophets confirm that this was a recognised, remembered crime.

Ezekiel's own longer oracle on Edom speaks of an 'ancient hatred', and Ezekiel 25:15 uses 'ancient hostility' of Philistia. The overlap shows the prophet thinking of old, handed-down grudges. In both places the accusation is not a single act but a settled posture toward God's people.

Moses sings of the LORD, 'Vengeance is Mine'. This is the root principle. When Edom and Philistia take vengeance in verses 12 and 15, they seize what the Torah reserves to the LORD, and verse 14 shows Him taking it back in His own name.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy 32:35 and applies it to believers: do not avenge yourselves, but leave room for God's wrath. The oracles of Ezekiel 25 show what 'leaving room' looks like, since the exiles are not asked to retaliate, only to wait for the LORD.

Shows envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon in Jerusalem planning revolt against Babylon. It helps explain the later gloating, for these were not distant observers but partners in the failed alliance who then cheered when Judah alone fell.

Baalis king of the Ammonites sent Ishmael to kill Gedaliah, the governor left over Judah's remnant. It gives a specific political action behind Ammon's attitude in Ezekiel 25:3 and 25:6, showing that gloating was followed by aggression.

The LORD says, 'I have heard the reproach of Moab and the insults of the Ammonites, who have taunted My people.' The verb 'heard' is the key. It confirms the principle behind Ezekiel 25, that the LORD hears what is said about His people, and ties these two nations together in one charge.

Promises that the restored house of David will 'possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name.' The sentence on Edom in Ezekiel 25:14 is not the last word. Acts 15:16-17 reads this promise as being fulfilled when the Gentiles turn to God.

Speaks of Philistia's pride being cut off and then of a remnant who 'will become a remnant for our God' and be like a clan in Judah. It supplies the other half of Ezekiel 25:16, where the Philistines are cut off: judgment removes the pride and leaves the possibility of a people for God.

Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and stops before the day of vengeance. Together with Ezekiel 25 it shows that the LORD's vengeance is real and is being held back while the year of the LORD's favour is proclaimed. The delay is mercy, not weakness.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world made good and a people made for blessing, and from the beginning the nations stand either with the promise or against it. God told Abraham, 'I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse', Genesis 12:3. Ezekiel 25 is that promise on the ground. These four nations are not judged for being foreign. They are judged for how they treated the people through whom God was working out His plan, and for taking to themselves what belongs to Him.

The story keeps returning to these peoples. Ammon and Moab come from Lot, whose rescue Abraham secured, and both are remembered for failing to meet Israel with food and water on the road from Egypt, Deuteronomy 23:3-4. Edom is Esau, the brother who lost the blessing and never forgave, Genesis 27:41. The Philistines were the great enemy of the judges and of Saul and David. Their hostility in Ezekiel's day is the latest stage of a family quarrel as old as Genesis.

The oracles answer a question the exiles are asking: has the God who made a covenant with us lost control of the nations? These oracles say no. The God who could permit Jerusalem's fall can also strip the pride of those who cheered. It sets up Ezekiel's later chapters, which end the nation oracles with Egypt and then promise Israel a land secure from every neighbour who treated her with contempt, Ezekiel 28:24 to 26.

The story moves forward in Christ. In the cross, the contempt of nations meets the Son and is answered with forgiveness, Luke 23:34. In the gospel, Edom's remnant, Philistia and the nations are gathered under David's greater Son, Amos 9:12 and Acts 15:16-17. And Isaiah 11:14, which pictures these same peoples brought under the Messiah's rule, finds its rest in the vision of every tribe and nation before the throne, Revelation 7:9.

The new creation is the end of all vengeance. 'Never again will they hunger', and God Himself will wipe away every tear, Revelation 7:16-17. In the world to come no one will gloat over another's ruin, and no enemy remains who needs to be answered, because the Judge has finished His work and every nation that comes in has come to know the LORD.

quiz.q: What specifically did Ammon do that provoked this judgment?

options.text: They exclaimed 'Aha!' in mockery when God's sanctuary was profaned and Judah went into exile.
options.note: Verse 3 names this exact mockery of the sanctuary's fall as the accusation.

options.text: They invaded Judah militarily before Babylon did.
options.note: The text does not describe a military invasion by Ammon; the sin named is gloating and contempt.

options.text: They refused to pay tribute to Babylon.
options.note: Not mentioned in this passage; the accusation concerns their response to Judah's fall, not tribute to Babylon.

options.text: They intermarried with Israelite families against the law.
options.note: Not the sin named here; the text specifically cites their mocking joy over the sanctuary's profanation.

quiz.q: What error did Moab and Seir make according to verse 8?

options.text: They said the house of Judah is like all the other nations, denying her unique covenant standing.
options.note: Verse 8 states this exact claim as Moab's provoking error.

options.text: They refused to acknowledge any god existed.
options.note: Their error was about Judah's status among the nations, not a denial of deity in general.

options.text: They demanded tribute from Jerusalem's temple treasury.
options.note: Not described in this text; the accusation is about how they characterized Judah's standing.

options.text: They built a rival temple to the LORD.
options.note: Not mentioned in this passage; the sin named is treating Judah as merely ordinary among the nations.

quiz.q: Why does the LORD say He will take vengeance on Edom and Philistia specifically?

options.text: Because they took vengeance on their own initiative, with malice, against Judah, so the LORD answers by reserving vengeance to Himself.
options.note: Verses 12 and 15 to 17 explicitly describe their vengeful, malicious actions and God's matching response.

options.text: Because they refused to send soldiers to help Judah.
options.note: Not what the text describes; the accusation is active vengeance and hostility, not a failure to help.

options.text: Because they worshiped different gods than Israel.
options.note: Idolatry is not the accusation named in this passage; the specific sin is vengeful violence and ancient hostility.

options.text: Because they were the largest of Judah's neighboring nations.
options.note: Size is irrelevant to the text's stated reason; the accusation is their vengeful, malicious conduct.

quiz.q: What refrain concludes each of the four oracles in this chapter?

options.text: That the nation judged will know that the LORD is God.
options.note: This refrain, in some form, closes every oracle: verses 5, 7, 11, and 17.

options.text: That the nation will be restored after seventy years.
options.note: No restoration promise appears in this chapter, unlike some other nation oracles elsewhere in Scripture.

options.text: That Israel will forgive each nation.
options.note: Forgiveness by Israel is not mentioned; the refrain concerns the nations knowing the LORD.

options.text: That each nation's gods will be publicly humiliated.
options.note: The oracles focus on the nations coming to know the LORD, not a specific humiliation of their gods.

quiz.q: What does this chapter reveal about the scope of God's justice?

options.text: It reaches every nation, not Israel alone, holding all peoples accountable for how they treat others in suffering.
options.note: Four different nations are judged here for related but distinct sins, showing justice with universal reach.

options.text: It applies only to nations that worship the LORD.
options.note: None of these four nations worshiped the LORD, yet all are held accountable, showing the opposite is true.

options.text: It is limited to nations that directly attacked Jerusalem militarily.
options.note: Some of these nations, like Moab, are judged for an attitude expressed in words, not direct military attack.

options.text: It applies only during the specific era of the Babylonian exile.
options.note: While historically fulfilled then, the principle of God's universal justice extends beyond that single era, as later Scripture affirms.

questions: Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia all responded to Judah's suffering with contempt, opportunism, or vengeance rather than compassion. Where are you tempted to feel satisfaction, rather than sorrow, at someone else's downfall?
Each oracle ends with 'they will know that I am the LORD.' Where in your own life has hardship or discipline become the very thing that made God more real and known to you?

Edom and Philistia took vengeance into their own hands rather than trusting God to repay evil. Where are you carrying a grudge or planning repayment that you need to release into God's hands instead, per Romans 12:19?

Moab dismissed Judah as 'like all the other nations,' denying her unique place in God's plan. Where might you be tempted to dismiss what God has specifically called or promised in your own life as ordinary or unremarkable?

These ancient enemy nations are, in the gospel, among the very peoples now invited to know the LORD through Christ. Who in your life feels as far outside God's reach as Ammon or Edom once did, and how might you extend the same grace that reached them?

translationNotes.note: Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim were Moab's fortified frontier cities; naming them specifically underscores that even Moab's most defended glory would be exposed.

The Cherethites were closely associated with the Philistines, sometimes serving as mercenaries even in David's own guard, 2 Samuel 8:18, making their inclusion here a sweeping judgment on the whole Philistine population.

The phrase 'by the hand of My people Israel' anticipates a later historical role for Israel, or for Israel's allies acting on the LORD's behalf, in Edom's downfall, rather than describing an immediate action in Ezekiel's own day.
